query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In an uncharacterized, single‐phase bcc high‐entropy alloy (HEA) that meets the five-element, ≥5 at.% each criterion, a moderate increase in atomic size mismatch—achieved by substituting a fraction of one constituent with an element having a larger atomic radius but similar chemical character—will enhance local lattice distortions, thereby increasing the electron–phonon coupling and raising the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) relative to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single‐phase bcc solid-solution HEA composed of at least five elements (none dominated by Nb–Ta or overly titanium‐rich), where each element is present at no less than 5 atomic percent.
generation.intervention: Substitute a controlled fraction (kept within single-phase limits) of one constituent element with an element of larger atomic radius (and comparable electronegativity) to deliberately increase the atomic size disparity without inducing secondary phases.
generation.conditions: Alloys are prepared by arc-melting under inert atmosphere to ensure full homogeneous mixing and a single bcc phase; subsequent superconductivity measurements are conducted at ambient pressure using standard electrical resistivity and magnetic susceptibility techniques.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced local lattice distortions (i.e. increased atomic size mismatch) that remain uniformly distributed in the bcc lattice.
generation.mechanism: The increased lattice distortion modifies the electronic density-of-states near the Fermi level and strengthens electron–phonon interactions, thereby increasing Tc as long as the disorder does not reach levels that induce localization or phase separation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will show a higher superconducting transition temperature compared to the baseline alloy. Although the precise magnitude is uncertain, a moderate (potentially on the order of a 1–2 K increase) increase in Tc is predicted under the controlled substitution.
generation.baseline: The original, unmodified bcc HEA without the additional element that induces extra atomic size mismatch.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to occur only if the substitution does not exceed the compositional window that maintains a homogeneous single-phase bcc structure under ambient pressure; beyond that window, phase separation or ordering may negate the effect.
generation.uncertainty: The exact increase in Tc is not precisely known and depends on the chosen substitution level and the delicate balance between enhanced electron–phonon coupling and disorder-induced scattering. Additionally, the chemical compatibility must be maintained to avoid secondary phases.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) the baseline bcc HEA and (2) a modified version in which a small, controlled fraction (e.g., 10 at.%) of one constituent is replaced by an element with a larger atomic radius while keeping the overall elemental concentrations above 5 at.% and maintaining a bcc solid solution. Confirm phase purity via X-ray diffraction. Then, measure their superconducting transition temperatures using electrical resistivity and magnetic susceptibility measurements under identical ambient conditions.
measurements: Magnetic susceptibility measurements (to verify bulk superconductivity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in Tc relative to the baseline, or if the substitution causes detectable phase separation or ordering (i.e. loss of the homogeneous bcc structure), then the hypothesis that increased atomic size mismatch enhances Tc is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Pressure is one of the variables that can uncover unexpected phenomena and properties (). For superconductors in particular, the pressure-induced enhancement of critical transition temperatures in copper-oxide and iron-pnictide superconductors (), the reemergence of superconductivity in the alkaline iron selenide () and heavy fermion superconductors (), pressure-induced superconductivity in H3S () and elements (, ), are examples. Therefore, looking for new phenomena in the superconducting HEA under pressure is of great interest. Here we report high-pressure studies on the superconducting HEA (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33, which has a critical transition temperature to the superconducting state (TC) of about 7.8 K at ambient pressure (, ). Our observations demonstrate that this alloy exhibits extraordinarily robust superconductivity––its zero-resistance superconducting state is still achieved even at a pressure of 190.6 GPa, or almost 2 megabars (1 Mbar = 1011 pascal), a pressure like that within the outer core of the earth. Such a superconductor with a highly robust zero-resistance state, existing continuously from 1 atm to geological pressures, is extremely unusual and is in fact unique

cited_evidence.text: The Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr system comprises five superconducting (SC) elements Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti and Zr, all belonging to the class of low-temperature superconductors, whereas Sc is non-superconducting at ambient pressure. The SC transition temperatures TC of pure metals are collected in Table 4, ranging from the highest TCNb= 9.20 K to the lowest TCHf= 0.12 K. We have studied the SC transition via electrical resistivity, specific heat and the Meissner effect. The experimental details are described in the Methods Section.
